title: PLOS study: 3 of 1,357 FDA-cleared AI medical devices tested on patient outcomes
subtitle: A University of Toronto team combed the FDA's authorized-devices list and found the evidence for clinical benefit is missing for almost all of them.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A study published August 19 in PLOS Digital Health, led by Rawan Abulibdeh of the University of Toronto, examined all 1,357 artificial-intelligence medical devices the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has cleared and traced how many were tested for real clinical effect. The numbers are unusually blunt for a peer-reviewed paper: 2.5% were tied to a registered prospective trial, 0.9% had posted trial results, 0.9% had peer-reviewed publications, and 0.2% — three devices — were tested for patient-centered outcomes such as mortality, morbidity, or hospital readmission.

FDA authorization for these devices runs through the 510(k) pathway, which requires evidence that a new device is 'substantially equivalent' to a predicate device already on the market. That standard is procedural, not clinical — it can be satisfied with retrospective test-set performance and does not require a trial showing that patients do better when clinicians use the device. That gap has always existed for hardware, but AI compresses it: an FDA-cleared triage model can change what a physician sees, when they see it, and how urgently they act, all without any published evidence that the outcome improves.

The finding lands as the FDA is running two proof-of-concept 'real-time clinical trial' pilots with Paradigm Health that would report endpoints to the agency continuously, and as Congress is being asked to update the 510(k) pathway for AI-enabled products. It also raises a specific procurement problem for hospitals: a system that has bought an FDA-cleared AI tool cannot assume the evidence supporting it answers 'does this help my patients?' — it usually answers 'does this predict the same thing the old tool did, on a curated retrospective dataset?' Those are different questions.

A note for learners: 'FDA-cleared' is a checkbox many AI healthcare vendors put on their marketing pages, and it means something — but it does not mean what a person outside medicine would assume. If you evaluate a healthcare AI product, ask whether it has a registered prospective trial (a clinicaltrials.gov ID) and whether that trial reports patient-centered outcomes. The paper's own methodology is a straightforward template: pull the device list, cross-reference the trials registry, and check the peer-reviewed literature. Try it on any AI device your provider mentions.
